title: Workspace isolation silently degrades to the mainline when worktree creation fails
description:
Workspace.AcquireAsync falls back to 'return RepoRoot' when both git worktree add attempts fail (Workspace.cs:62,65). The caller cannot tell the difference: the implement station then edits the USER'S CHECKOUT directly, with a thick profile and bypassPermissions.

Two compounding problems:
1. Concurrent 'git worktree add' from the claim loop is not serialised, and concurrent branch creation is exactly what makes the add fail (ref lock contention) — so the fallback is most likely precisely when concurrency > 1.
2. Once one item works in place, a sibling item's IntegrateAsync sees a dirty mainline and returns 'the working tree has uncommitted changes', which escalates to Blocked. Verified work is stranded by an unrelated item.

This violates SPEC.md section 10 ('Workspace isolation per item; mainline is only touched by Integrate after gates pass') and is the leading suspect for the known flake PipelineTests.Two_independent_ready_items_are_both_claimed_and_completed (~1 in 9, and the test now asserts Blocked==0 first precisely because the failure mode was unclear).
design: Two changes. (a) Serialise worktree acquisition with a semaphore on Workspace, the same way _integrateGate serialises merges — worktree add is short, so this costs nothing. (b) Make the fallback explicit rather than silent: if a worktree genuinely cannot be created, fail the station with a message naming git's error instead of returning RepoRoot. Working in the user's checkout must be an opt-in for the no-git case (Workspace.IsGitRepo == false), not a silent error path.
acceptance_criteria: A test forces 'git worktree add' to fail and asserts AcquireAsync surfaces the failure rather than returning RepoRoot; a second test acquires two worktrees concurrently and asserts both are distinct directories under WorktreesDir.

title: Command output is truncated at the head while every consumer formats the tail
description:
Shell.ReadAsync stops appending once the sink reaches MaxCapturedOutputChars (Shell.cs:255), so a long capture retains the FIRST 64k and discards everything after it.

Every consumer then takes the tail, and documents why:
- ToolchainRunner.Explain: 'The tail is where compilers and test runners put the thing that went wrong' — takes output[^2500..]
- DeterministicVerifier.Tail: 'trimmed to the tail — where the error normally is' — takes s[^1200..]

For any build or test log over 64k the two disagree: the tail-slice operates on the head-truncated buffer, so the implement station is fed bytes ~62.8k-64k of the log — the middle — labelled as the error. The actual compiler error or test failure at the end of the log is gone.

This directly degrades the repair loop: LastFailure is what ImplementStation injects as 'The previous attempt was rejected. Fix exactly this:'. Feeding it the middle of a build log wastes a full implement retry.
design: Make ReadAsync retain the tail: keep appending and trim the StringBuilder from the front when it exceeds the cap (e.g. sink.Remove(0, overflow) after each append), or buffer into a fixed-size ring. Note the interaction with BeadsCli.ReadOrReportTruncation, which currently reasons about head-truncation to detect a cut JSON document — that check needs updating in the same change, since tail-retention cuts the START of the JSON instead.
acceptance_criteria: A test runs a command emitting well over MaxCapturedOutputChars where the final line is a unique marker, and asserts the marker is present in ShellResult.Stdout.

title: AgentRunner and ResponseCache counters race under concurrency
description:
AgentRunner.TotalCostUsd, TotalUsage, Calls and CacheHits are plain mutable auto-properties updated with += and ++ (AgentRunner.cs:66-68). ResponseCache.Hits/Misses are the same. One AgentRunner instance is shared by every station via FactoryServices.Runner, so with MaxConcurrency > 1 these are unsynchronised read-modify-write from multiple threads.

Consequence: lost updates. OrchestratorReport.CostUsd, ModelCalls, CacheHits and every token figure in 'factory status' and the run summary are silently understated. Because this is the number an operator uses to decide whether the factory is affordable, a wrong figure is worse than no figure.

Latent today only because Blueprint.DefaultMaxConcurrency is 1 — it becomes real the moment concurrency is raised (see the worktree-sync work).
design: Convert the decimal/TokenUsage accumulators to lock-guarded updates (a single Lock around a small mutation block is simpler here than Interlocked, because TokenUsage is a record and decimal has no Interlocked overload). Convert Calls/CacheHits to Interlocked.Increment with volatile reads. Same treatment for ResponseCache.Hits/Misses.
acceptance_criteria: A test runs N concurrent AgentRunner.RunAsync calls against a fake transport with a known per-call cost and asserts Calls == N and TotalCostUsd == N * cost exactly.

title: Structured-output repair retry is dead code; one malformed payload fails the item
description:
AgentRunner.RunStructuredAsync implements the schema-repair retry described in SPEC.md Phase 2 ('StructuredAgent<T>: --json-schema -> typed T, with repair retry'). It has ZERO callers anywhere in src or tests.

Every station instead calls AgentStation.InvokeAsync and then run.TryStructured<T> directly (DecomposeStation, PlanStation, ReviewStation). When TryStructured fails they return StationResult.Failed('unparseable decomposition/plan/review'), which routes to the fail path — no repair attempt is ever made.

This is the mechanism behind the 'decompose: stop_sequence' and 'error_max_budget_usd' failures in HANDOFF.md: a truncated or fenced JSON reply kills the item outright when one cheap repair round would recover it.
design: Either route the three structured stations through RunStructuredAsync, or lift its repair logic into AgentStation.InvokeAsync so every schema-carrying call gets one repair round. Prefer the latter: InvokeAsync is already the single choke point that records the RunRecord, so the repair attempt lands in the ledger as evidence instead of vanishing. Ensure the repair attempt's cost is charged (see the retry-spend bug — same root).
acceptance_criteria: A test drives the decompose station through a transport that returns fenced/prose-wrapped JSON on the first call and clean JSON on the repair call, and asserts the station succeeds and two runs are recorded.

title: Daily budget exhaustion blocks items instead of parking them until the window rolls
description:
BudgetGuard.EnsureCanSpend raises BudgetExhaustedException for the daily scope, and Orchestrator turns any BudgetExhaustedException into BlockAsync (Orchestrator.cs:348). Blocked requires a human 'factory activate' to clear.

But a daily ceiling is a RATE limit, not a terminal condition: it clears by itself when the UTC day rolls (BudgetGuard.RollDay). Treating it like a permanent blocker is what produces the single largest category of stuck work — 11 items currently sit blocked on 'Budget exhausted for daily' per HANDOFF.md.

The factory already has the right pattern for this: UsageGovernor.ShouldHold parks dispatch for a rate limit and resumes without human involvement.
design: Distinguish rate-shaped ceilings (daily, evolution/daily) from terminal ceilings (per-item). BudgetExhaustedException already carries Scope. For a rate-shaped scope, return the item to Ready and have the orchestrator hold dispatch until the window rolls — the same shape as the throttled/holdFor branch in RunAsync — rather than transitioning to Blocked. Keep per-item exhaustion as Blocked: that one genuinely needs a human to raise the ceiling.
acceptance_criteria: A test with a daily ceiling already spent asserts the item ends Ready (not Blocked) and that the orchestrator logged a hold rather than requiring activate.

title: Retried model-call spend is never charged to the budget or the ledger
description:
AgentRunner.RunAsync loops up to MaxRetries+1 attempts (default 4) and adds every attempt's cost to its own TotalCostUsd (AgentRunner.cs:67). AgentStation.InvokeAsync then records only the FINAL attempt's result.CostUsd (Station.cs:216) into BudgetGuard.Record and the BudgetConsumed event.

Consequence: up to three attempts' spend per station call escapes both the per-item ceiling and the daily ceiling. BudgetGuard therefore under-counts, EnsureCanSpend lets work through that the factory has already paid for, and JsonlRunHistory.ForBudget restores the wrong totals on restart because there is no event carrying the lost spend.

Worst case per station call: 4x the recorded cost. This compounds silently across every retried run.
design: Have the transport-facing layer report per-attempt spend rather than only the terminal result. Either (a) return an attempt list / cumulative cost on AgentRunResult and have InvokeAsync record the cumulative figure, or (b) give AgentRunner a callback invoked per attempt that Station wires to Budget.Record + a BudgetConsumed event. Option (b) keeps the ledger event count honest (one BudgetConsumed per actual model call), which is what the evaluator mines.
acceptance_criteria: A test drives AgentRunner through a transport that fails transiently twice then succeeds, and asserts BudgetGuard.SpentOn(item) equals the sum of all three attempts' costs, not just the last.

title: Model-authored regex runs with no match timeout in the verify station
description:
DeterministicVerifier.RunCommandAsync evaluates ExpectStdoutMatch with Regex.IsMatch(run.Stdout, expectMatch) (DeterministicVerifier.cs:79). The pattern comes from model output (VerificationDto), the input is up to 64k of captured command output, and the call specifies neither RegexOptions.NonBacktracking nor a matchTimeout.

A pattern with catastrophic backtracking — trivially produced by a model writing something like (a+)+b — hangs the verify station indefinitely on a thread-pool thread. There is no station-level timeout above it: VerifyStation awaits DeterministicVerifier.VerifyAsync with only ctx.Ct, and the regex call does not observe cancellation.

Unlike the command itself, which at least has a timeoutSeconds, the regex has no bound at all.
design: Pass a matchTimeout to Regex.IsMatch (a second or two is generous for a stdout match), or compile with RegexOptions.NonBacktracking where the pattern permits it. On RegexMatchTimeoutException, fail the criterion with a message naming the pattern as the cause rather than letting it surface as an unhandled station exception.
acceptance_criteria: A test supplies a catastrophic-backtracking pattern against a long stdout and asserts the criterion fails with a timeout message within a bounded wall time.

title: The toolchain baseline is recaptured after every integrate, serialising a full mainline build behind every item
description:
Each successful integrate merges into the mainline, which moves HEAD. CheckStation.RunCheckedAsync then calls GetOrRecaptureBaselineAsync (CheckStation.cs:79), which compares the cached baseline's commit against the current SHA, finds it stale, and re-runs the ENTIRE toolchain on the mainline before the item's own checks run.

All of it happens inside the factory-wide ToolchainGate, which is exclusive. So per item the serialised critical path is: mainline build + mainline test + worktree build + worktree test. With the dotnet defaults (build 900s, test 1800s) and ToolchainRunner.RunAsync retrying each failed check once, the worst case inside the exclusive gate is ~90 minutes for a single item.

Net effect: raising --concurrency buys nothing for the dominant cost, because every item queues behind the same lock, and each one pays for a fresh mainline baseline that the previous item's merge invalidated.
design: The mainline baseline only needs recapturing when the mainline actually changed in a way that could alter check outcomes — and the factory knows when it merged, because IntegrateStation did it. Options, cheapest first: (a) after a successful integrate, carry the just-verified worktree results forward as the new baseline for the new HEAD instead of recomputing them (the worktree that just merged cleanly IS the new mainline); (b) narrow the gate so only the item's own checks are serialised and baseline recapture happens once per orchestrator run; (c) make baseline recapture incremental — only re-run checks whose inputs the merge touched.
acceptance_criteria: A test runs two items to completion through integrate and asserts the toolchain executes at most one mainline baseline capture, not one per item.

title: The ledger is re-read and re-parsed in full on every query
description:
JsonlRunHistory has no index, no in-memory projection and no snapshot. Every one of these does a complete file read plus JSON deserialisation of every event:
- Runs() -> ReadFrom(0).OfType<RunCompleted>() (JsonlRunHistory.cs:115), which backs RunsForItem, RunsForStation and Totals
- ForBudget() -> Replay() -> full read + full fold
- Champions() -> Replay() -> full read + full fold
- the constructor itself, to compute _seq

Cost at the call sites:
- FactoryHost.Open performs at least three full passes (ctor, FactoryState.Replay, ForBudget) before it returns. Every CLI command pays this, including read-only ones like 'factory ls' and 'factory status'.
- EvolutionService.RunAsync calls RunsForStation once PER STATION (six evolvable stations = six full passes) plus one more for FailureTraces.
- Commands.Show adds another via RunsForItem.

The ledger is append-only and never compacted, so this is O(total history) forever and grows monotonically with every gate evaluation, state change and run. It is the single largest scaling limit in the codebase.
design: Keep the folded FactoryState as the read model and serve queries from it instead of re-reading the file — the fold is already maintained live by FactoryServices.Record and LedgerMirroringWorkItemStore. Concretely: hold a run index (by item id and by station id) inside FactoryState alongside _runs, and have JsonlRunHistory's query methods consult a cached projection that is invalidated only by Append. Longer term, add periodic snapshotting (write a state snapshot every N events and replay only the tail) so open cost stops being proportional to total history.
acceptance_criteria: A benchmark test writes a ledger of 50k events and asserts FactoryHost.Open performs a single full pass, and that RunsForStation does not re-read the file.

title: Model-authored shell commands are executed unsandboxed
description:
AcceptanceCriterion verification of kind 'command' or 'tests' carries a raw command string that originates in model output: the intake and decompose stations emit VerificationDto.Command against Schemas (Contracts.cs), which becomes CommandVerification/TestsPassVerification via ToDomain. DeterministicVerifier.RunCommandAsync passes that string straight to Shell.RunAsync, which executes it as '/bin/sh -c <command>' (Shell.cs:115) in the item's worktree.

There is no allowlist, no denylist, no argument validation and no sandbox anywhere on that path.

SPEC.md section 10 states: 'Blast-radius limits — permission mode is per-station, and destructive shell patterns are denied by default.' The per-station permission mode exists (AgentProfile.PermissionMode). The destructive-pattern denial does not exist at all.

This is the one place where a model's output is executed as code with no gate whatsoever, and it runs on every verify station execution — the most frequently repeated step in the pipeline.
design: Add a deny policy in front of DeterministicVerifier's command execution. Minimum viable: a configurable denylist of destructive patterns (rm -rf outside the worktree, dd, mkfs, curl|sh, writes outside the worktree root, sudo) evaluated before Shell.RunAsync, with a refusal recorded as a failed criterion naming the rejected pattern. Better: run criterion commands with a constrained environment and working directory, and treat anything that escapes the worktree as a failure. The policy belongs on the Blueprint so it is declarative like the rest of the safety surface.
acceptance_criteria: A test files an item whose acceptance criterion is a destructive command and asserts the verifier refuses it, records a failed criterion naming the policy, and never spawns a shell.

title: CheckStation writes Blocked outside the state machine on a toolchain mismatch
description:
CheckStation.ResolveMismatchAsync returns a StationResult carrying 'Item = ctx.Item with { State = WorkItemState.Blocked, LastError = reason }' (CheckStation.cs:125).

The orchestrator applies that via host.Update(updated), which is a plain WorkItemUpdated write. That bypasses IWorkItemStore.Transition entirely, so:
- WorkItemStates.CanTransition is never consulted (an illegal transition is written without complaint)
- no WorkItemStateChanged event is emitted, so the ledger has no record of WHY the item was blocked and no reason string
- with the beads provider, BeadMapper sees a status change arriving through the update path rather than the transition path

Worse, the result also has GatePassed=false, so the orchestrator continues into the gate-failure branch and may transition the now-Blocked item again — to Failed via FailAsync, or to Blocked a second time via BlockAsync. The item's recorded history is then incoherent.

Every other station signals 'a human must look at this' by returning GateFailed and letting the blueprint's EscalateToHuman flag decide; CheckStation is the only one that writes the state itself.
design: Drop the Item mutation from ResolveMismatchAsync and return StationResult.GateFailed(reason). Mark the check station EscalateToHuman in Blueprint.Standard() so the orchestrator's own BlockAsync path handles it — that routes through Transition, checks legality, and emits WorkItemStateChanged with the reason.
acceptance_criteria: A test forces a toolchain mismatch with no remediation available and asserts the item ends Blocked, that a WorkItemStateChanged event carrying the mismatch reason is in the ledger, and that no second transition follows.

title: HeartbeatTimer.Stop and Dispose do not drain an in-flight tick
description:
HeartbeatTimer.OnTick fires on a thread-pool thread and launches the callback fire-and-forget ('_ = RunTickAsync()'). Stop() only calls _timer.Change(Infinite, Infinite) (HeartbeatTimer.cs:39) and Dispose() calls _timer.Dispose() without the WaitHandle overload. Neither waits for a tick already in flight.

Two consequences:
1. This is the root cause of the known flake HeartbeatTimerTests.StopHaltsFurtherInvocations. The test reads the counter immediately after Stop(); a tick that fired just before Stop() but had not yet incremented then lands inside the 100ms window, and afterStop != count. Nothing about the test is wrong — the type genuinely offers no drain guarantee.
2. Operationally: Orchestrator.RunAsync calls leases.Stop() and returns. An in-flight RefreshClaimsAsync can therefore run after the orchestrator has finished, calling Heartbeat on a store the host is about to dispose.

Named in HANDOFF.md as one of two flakes, and flakes here are expensive: the check station gates on dotnet test, so a flake can record a false regression or poison the toolchain baseline and silently switch a gate off.
design: Track the in-flight tick task and have Stop() await it (with a bounded timeout), or expose StopAsync. For Dispose, use the Timer.Dispose(WaitHandle) overload and wait on the handle so callbacks are drained before the type is considered disposed. Keep Dispose non-throwing and idempotent as it is today.
acceptance_criteria: HeartbeatTimerTests.StopHaltsFurtherInvocations passes 200 consecutive runs; a new test asserts that a tick started before Stop() has completed by the time Stop() returns.

title: Delegated child-factory spend never reaches the ledger and is lost on restart
description:
DelegateStation charges child spend to the parent's in-memory BudgetGuard (DelegateStation.cs:73) but emits no BudgetConsumed event — unlike AgentStation.InvokeAsync, which records one for every model call.

JsonlRunHistory.ForBudget rebuilds the budget accumulators exclusively from RunCompleted records. The child's runs live in the CHILD's ledger, and the parent records only DelegationStarted/DelegationCompleted. So on the next FactoryHost.Open the parent's daily and per-item totals come back with every dollar of delegated spend missing.

The code comment claims 'Child spend rolls up to the parent's budget so a composite cannot exceed its ceiling by hiding cost inside its children' — true within one process, false across a restart.
design: Record a BudgetConsumed event alongside the Budget.Record call in DelegateStation, and teach ForBudget to fold BudgetConsumed for scopes it cannot derive from RunCompleted. Alternatively give DelegationCompleted (which already carries ChildCostUsd) a fold in the budget restore path — that avoids a second event type carrying the same fact.
acceptance_criteria: A test delegates to a child factory that spends a known amount, closes and reopens the parent host, and asserts BudgetGuard.SpentOn(parentItem) still includes the child's cost.

title: An agent's reasoned blocker report is discarded and retried as a failed run
description:
When the implement station produces no file changes, ImplementStation returns GateFailed('no file changes were produced. ' + the model's text capped at 800 chars) (PipelineStations.cs:195). The orchestrator treats that like any other gate failure: increment attempts, route back to implement via OnFail, and after Retries fail or block the item.

But there are two very different situations behind 'no file changes':
- the agent tried and produced nothing useful — retrying is right
- the agent examined the work and reported a REASON it cannot proceed (missing dependency, contradictory requirement, a decision that needs a human) — retrying just pays for the same conclusion again, up to Retries times, and then discards it

HANDOFF.md counts 3 items currently stuck in exactly the second case and names it the second-biggest autonomy defect: 'There is no escalation path carrying a reason.' The model's explanation IS carried into Detail, but nothing distinguishes it from a mechanical failure, so nothing acts on it.
design: Give the implement station a way to say 'blocked, and here is why' as a first-class outcome rather than a gate failure. Cheapest path: attach a small structured schema to the implement station's terminal message (or a follow-up thin classification call on the no-changes path only) that distinguishes 'could not proceed because X' from 'produced nothing'. Route the former straight to Blocked with the reason as LastError, skipping the retry budget entirely. This pairs with the budget-parking change — both are about ending a run in a state a human can act on rather than a state a human must rescue.
acceptance_criteria: A test drives implement through a transport that returns no file changes plus an explicit blocker explanation, and asserts the item goes to Blocked on the first attempt with the explanation preserved in LastError, with no retry dispatched.

title: Nothing prevents two factories running against one repository
description:
FactoryPaths.LockFile is declared (FactoryPaths.cs:20) and referenced NOWHERE else in src or tests. There is no process lock of any kind.

HANDOFF.md compensates with an operating note — 'Run one factory at a time per repository' — and also states the opposite is routine: 'Other agents write to this repository concurrently — a JetBrains Rider agent and Claude Code desktop sessions, some with permission checks disabled. This is expected and allowed.'

Two concrete failure modes when that note is not honoured:
1. JsonlRunHistory computes _seq once in its constructor and opens the file with FileShare.ReadWrite. Two processes appending both continue from their own snapshot of the maximum, producing DUPLICATE Seq values. ReadFrom filters with 'evt.Seq > afterSeq', so a duplicate-sequence ledger silently drops events on incremental reads and FactoryState.LastSeq becomes meaningless.
2. Workspace._integrateGate is an instance SemaphoreSlim, so it serialises merges within one process only. Two processes merging into the same mainline race on the index and refs.

The guard exists as a filename and a sentence in a document.
design: Take an exclusive advisory lock on FactoryPaths.LockFile at FactoryHost.Open (an OS file lock, not a lock file whose existence is checked — the latter strands on a crash), and fail with a message naming the holding pid. For the ledger sequence specifically, either derive Seq from the file at append time under the lock, or stop relying on Seq for ordering and use byte offset. Read-only commands should be able to open without the exclusive lock.
acceptance_criteria: A test opens a second FactoryHost against a repo already open and asserts it fails with a message naming the holder; a second test appends from two writers and asserts no duplicate Seq values.

title: WorktreeSyncService is implemented and tested but wired to nothing
description:
WorktreeSyncService and SyncOutcome are complete, documented and covered by WorktreeSyncServiceTests — and have no callers in src. Grep confirms the only references outside their own files are in the test.

It exists to solve the third autonomy defect named in HANDOFF.md: 'Branches never sync with a moved mainline. Each item worktree is branched at claim time and merged with --no-ff at integrate; nothing rebases. Two items touching one file conflict deterministically.' That is also why Blueprint.DefaultMaxConcurrency is pinned to 1, with the comment 'Raise this only once integrate rebases before merging.'

Blocking gap: SyncAsync requires a baseCommit argument, and nothing records one. Workspace.AcquireAsync creates the worktree from HEAD but never persists which commit that was. WorkItem has a Worktree field but no base-commit field.
design: Record the base commit at worktree acquisition (either on the WorkItem as local run state, or read it back with git rev-parse when needed), then call WorktreeSyncService before the check station and again before integrate. On SyncOutcome.Conflict, route to implement with the conflict as LastFailure rather than failing outright. Once this lands and is proven, DefaultMaxConcurrency can be raised — that is the payoff and should be part of the same change's acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: An integration test runs two items that touch the same file, with the first merging before the second reaches integrate, and asserts the second syncs and integrates cleanly rather than conflicting.

title: A large prompt can deadlock the transport until the 30-minute timeout
description:
CliAgentTransport.RunAsync awaits the complete stdin write before it begins reading stdout: 'await proc.StandardInput.WriteAsync(request.Prompt.AsMemory(), token)' (CliAgentTransport.cs:65), and the stdout ReadLineAsync loop only starts afterwards. Only stderr is drained concurrently.

If the prompt exceeds the stdin pipe buffer (~64k on Linux) AND the CLI emits enough stream-json to fill its own stdout buffer before consuming all of stdin, both processes block: the harness waiting to finish writing, the CLI waiting for its output to be read. Nothing breaks the cycle until timeoutCts fires at 30 minutes, and the run is then reported as a timeout.

The irony is that stdin was chosen precisely to carry large prompts — the class comment says 'The prompt goes in on stdin rather than as an argument, so prompt size is not bounded by the OS argument limit.' The thick implement station assembles prompt text plus plan plus a 3000-char failure excerpt, and ReviewStation appends a diff capped at ContextByteCap (24,000 default, and configurable higher).
design: Start the stdout reader before or concurrently with the stdin write. Kick off the ReadLineAsync loop as a task, then write stdin and close it, then await the reader — the same pattern already used for stderr via DrainAsync.
acceptance_criteria: A test drives the transport with a prompt larger than the pipe buffer against a fake CLI that writes substantial output before draining stdin, and asserts the call completes promptly rather than timing out.

title: External cancellation is reported to callers as a command timeout
description:
Shell.ExecCoreAsync links the caller's CancellationToken with the timeout token, then catches OperationCanceledException from either source and unconditionally returns 'new ShellResult(124, ..., TimedOut: true)' (Shell.cs:76).

So a graceful drain or Ctrl-C during a check or verify step is indistinguishable from the command exceeding its timeout. Downstream that becomes a gate failure with the text 'timed out after Ns' rather than a cancellation: ToolchainRunner.Explain reports a timeout, and the item can be routed back to implement — burning a retry and tokens — for a shutdown the operator requested.

Orchestrator.ProcessItemAsync has a correct OperationCanceledException handler that requeues the item as Ready, but it never sees the exception because Shell swallowed it.
design: Inspect the outer token in the catch: if ct.IsCancellationRequested, rethrow the OperationCanceledException so it propagates to the orchestrator's cancellation path; only synthesise the 124/TimedOut result when the timeout token fired. CliAgentTransport already does exactly this distinction ('var reason = ct.IsCancellationRequested ? "cancelled" : ...') — mirror it.
acceptance_criteria: A test cancels the caller's token mid-command and asserts Shell.RunAsync throws OperationCanceledException rather than returning TimedOut, and that the orchestrator requeues the item as Ready.

title: Every ledger append fsyncs under a global lock
description:
JsonlRunHistory.Append calls _out.Flush(true) (JsonlRunHistory.cs:39) — flush-to-disk, not just flush-to-OS — while holding the instance lock, for every single event.

Events are not rare: RunStarted, RunCompleted, GateEvaluated, CriteriaVerified, BudgetConsumed and a WorkItemUpdated per station hop, per item. Under concurrency every station serialises behind that fsync.

Durability here is worth something — the ledger is what makes the factory crash-resumable — but per-event fsync is the strictest possible setting, and ReadFrom already tolerates a torn final line ('Torn or unreadable line: skip it and keep the rest of the history'). That tolerance means the design already accepts losing the last record on a hard kill, which is precisely what a weaker flush policy would risk.
design: Make the durability policy explicit and tunable rather than maximal by default: batch flushes (flush on a short timer or every N events), or use Flush(false) for routine events and reserve Flush(true) for the ones a restart genuinely must not lose. Measure first — this may be a non-issue on the target hardware, in which case close it as measured-and-fine rather than guessing.
acceptance_criteria: A benchmark records appends/second before and after; a crash-resumption test still passes with the new policy.

title: Shell progress callbacks are process-global mutable statics that nested factories clobber
description:
Shell.OnCommandStarted and OnCommandCompleted are static fields (Shell.cs:26-27). Orchestrator's constructor assigns them (Orchestrator.cs) and Dispose() sets them back to null unconditionally.

This breaks under composition. DelegateStation opens a child FactoryHost and creates a child Orchestrator, whose constructor OVERWRITES the parent orchestrator's callbacks with its own. When the child finishes and is disposed, its Dispose() nulls the statics outright — so the PARENT orchestrator loses its progress hooks for the rest of the run, with nothing restoring them.

Note on history: as of the analyzer/guardrails phase on master, DelegateStation now correctly wraps the child in 'using var orchestrator = child.CreateOrchestrator();' (CA2000). That fixed the leaked ProcessExit handler — but it also turned the clobber from latent into active: before the fix the child was never disposed, so it never nulled the parent's hooks. Disposing the child is right; the global mutable statics are what make it harmful.

The callbacks currently only feed _lastProgressUtc, which nothing reads, so the damage is still latent overall. It becomes real as soon as the stall detection those callbacks exist for is implemented (see the dead-scaffolding issue).
design: Make the progress hook per-orchestrator rather than per-process. The AsyncLocal CurrentItemId is already the right shape; pair it with an AsyncLocal or a scoped listener registry so a nested orchestrator's hooks nest and unwind instead of overwriting and nulling. Minimum stopgap if the full change is deferred: have Orchestrator.Dispose restore the previous delegate it captured at construction rather than assigning null, so nesting at least unwinds correctly.
acceptance_criteria: A test runs a parent factory delegating to a child and asserts the parent's progress callbacks still fire after the child completes, and that no ProcessExit handler is left registered.

title: EvolutionService materialises every failed gate detail ever recorded to use twelve
description:
EvolutionService.FailureTraces() iterates the entire ledger (EvolutionService.cs:105) and appends every GateEvaluated{Passed:false}.Detail into per-station lists, then reverses each list. EvolutionLoop.ProposeAsync then uses failureTraces.Take(12).

So the whole failure history is read, parsed, allocated and reversed on every evolution pass to feed twelve strings into a prompt. Combined with RunsForStation being called once per station, an evolve pass costs roughly (stations + 1) full ledger passes.
design: Read the ledger backwards, or cap accumulation per station at the number actually consumed (keep a bounded ring of the most recent N failures per station while scanning). Fold into the ledger-index work — once runs and events are indexed, this becomes a bounded query.
acceptance_criteria: A test with a large synthetic ledger asserts FailureTraces allocates a bounded number of strings per station regardless of history size.

title: Backlog size is hard-capped by the 64k shell output limit
description:
BeadsCli reads bd's JSON through Shell.Run, which stops capturing at Shell.MaxCapturedOutputChars (64,000). BeadsWorkItemStore.All() calls 'bd list --json' and deserialises whatever came back.

The code already knows this happens: BeadsCli.ReadOrReportTruncation exists specifically to turn the resulting JsonException into 'bd ... produced more than 64000 characters, so its JSON was truncated before it could be read.'

So past roughly 64k of backlog JSON — a few hundred items with descriptions and acceptance criteria — All() throws, GuardedWorkItemStore converts it to WorkItemStoreException, and the factory halts. The diagnostic is good; the ceiling is still a hard wall with no workaround short of shrinking the backlog.

This bites exactly when the factory succeeds at filing its own improvement work.
design: Stop reading bulk JSON through a fixed-size capture buffer. Either stream bd's stdout directly to the JSON deserialiser rather than buffering to a string, or page the listing (bd list supports filtering/limits) and concatenate. Streaming is the real fix and removes the cap entirely; paging is the smaller change.
acceptance_criteria: A test drives All() against a fake bd emitting well over 64k of valid JSON and asserts every item is returned.

title: The beads backlog spawns a bd process per operation; a transition costs three
description:
BeadsCli.Exec shells out to the bd executable synchronously for every single operation. The call counts compound:
- Update = one write, then ReconcileDependencies (BeadsWorkItemStore.cs:22) which issues its own Get to diff dependency edges = 2 processes
- Transition = Update (2) + Note (1) = 3 processes
- AddDependency on failure adds another Get via EdgeTypeJoining

The orchestrator calls host.Update(run.Item with { Station = stationId }) at EVERY station hop (Orchestrator.cs, the while loop), plus a Transition at claim, supersede, complete, fail and block. For a seven-station pipeline with retries that is dozens of process spawns per item, each carrying process-start latency plus Dolt open cost.

ReconcileDependencies is the avoidable half: it re-reads the bead on every update purely to diff DependsOn, which changes only when decompose wires up children — i.e. almost never.
design: Skip ReconcileDependencies when the caller's DependsOn is unchanged from the copy already in the fold (the mirror has it), falling back to the read only when they differ or the item is unknown locally. Separately, consider batching the station-hop Update: the Station field is local run state, so it may not need a backlog round-trip at all — LocalRunState already exists for exactly this distinction.
acceptance_criteria: A test runs one item through the full pipeline against a counting BeadsCli fake and asserts the bd invocation count is bounded and does not grow with station count for items whose dependencies never change.

title: FactoryState.Items and Runs copy the whole collection on every property read
description:
FactoryState.Items allocates a full Dictionary copy under the lock on every access (FactoryState.cs:20); Runs and Champions do the same for their collections.

Hot callers make this quadratic:
- LedgerMirroringWorkItemStore.ItemOf calls state.Items.GetValueOrDefault(id) on EVERY mirror operation — so every Add/Update/Transition/TryClaim/Release copies the entire item dictionary to look up one key.
- Commands.List calls state.SpentFor(i.Id) per item, and SpentFor scans all runs under the lock: O(items x runs).
- Orchestrator's claim loop reaches Dispatchable() every poll, which copies, filters and sorts all items.

Correct as written — snapshots are deliberate, and the comment says so — but the snapshot is being paid for lookups that need one entry.
design: Add lock-guarded single-entry accessors that do not copy: TryGetItem(id, out item), SpentFor already exists but should consult a per-item run index rather than scanning. Keep the copying properties for genuine enumeration callers. Pair this with the run index from the ledger-performance issue — the two share a data structure.
acceptance_criteria: A test asserts LedgerMirroringWorkItemStore performs no full-dictionary copy per operation (e.g. via a FactoryState subclass counting Items accesses), and a benchmark shows Commands.List is linear in item count.

title: Remove dead scaffolding whose tests assert nothing real
description:
Three pieces of scaffolding are declared, documented as not-yet-wired, and consulted by nothing:

1. Orchestrator.StallThreshold and _lastProgressUtc. The XML docs say so outright: 'Not yet consulted anywhere — reserved for a later change.' TouchProgress writes into _lastProgressUtc from six call sites and Shell's static hooks feed it, but nothing ever reads the dictionary — and nothing removes entries either, so it grows for the life of the process. RuntimeTests.OrchestratorStallThresholdTests asserts the property returns its constructor argument, which is a test of C# property assignment, not of factory behaviour.

2. ToolchainBaseline.CapturedCommitSha, documented as 'Not wired up to any staleness comparison — Commit remains the source of truth for that.' It is written and never read.

3. WorkItem.SpentUsd, which HANDOFF.md already calls vestigial: FactoryState.SpentFor is the truth, and WorkItemUpdated replaces the record wholesale so the accumulated value reads as zero for most items.

Cost of leaving them: they read as implemented features. The StallThreshold tests in particular are the kind that make a suite look greener than it is — the same failure mode HANDOFF.md records as 'Status assertions let three criticals through a green suite'.
design: Either finish or delete, per item. StallThreshold: the stall check is genuinely wanted, so prefer finishing it — a stalled-item check against _lastProgressUtc in the orchestrator poll loop, plus eviction on item completion — and replace the property-assignment tests with one that observes an actual stall being detected. CapturedCommitSha and WorkItem.SpentUsd: delete. SpentUsd requires touching LocalRunState.CarriedInto, which carries it across the store boundary, so it is the largest of the three.
acceptance_criteria: No property in the codebase is documented as 'not consulted anywhere'; the stall check either detects a stalled item in a test or the field is gone; dotnet test stays green.

title: Prompt promotion lineage is recorded as placeholder text
description:
SPEC.md section 7 promises 'Every promotion and demotion is a ledger event, so prompt lineage is fully auditable.' The events are emitted but their from-version fields are not real versions:

- PromptPromoted uses '_s.State.Champions.GetValueOrDefault(station.Id) ?? "v?"'. State.Champions is populated ONLY by these same events, so on the first promotion for a station it is empty and the literal string 'v?' is recorded as the previous champion.
- PromptDemoted passes the literal 'challenger' as the from-version (EvolutionService.cs:74).

So the lineage chain cannot be reconstructed: the first link is 'v?' and every demotion records a word rather than an identifier. The registry itself knows the correct values — PromptRegistry.Champion(stationId) and Pointer(stationId).Challenger — they are simply not read at the point the event is built.

Low operational impact today because HANDOFF.md notes 'The evolution loop has still never promoted a prompt.' It matters the moment it does, and it is cheap to fix before there is history to migrate.
design: Read the outgoing champion's version from PromptRegistry BEFORE calling SetChampion, and pass the real challenger version into PromptDemoted from the outcome the loop already has. EvolutionLoop.RunStationAsync holds both values locally (via prompts.Champion(stationId) and prompts.Routing(stationId).Challenger — note Pointer was renamed to Routing in the analyzer phase); surface them on EvolutionOutcome so EvolutionService does not have to re-derive them.
acceptance_criteria: A test promotes then demotes a challenger and asserts the ledger's PromptPromoted/PromptDemoted events carry real station/version identifiers on both ends, with no 'v?' or 'challenger' literals.
